note: First taxonomy joining input level exploits to protocol level vulnerabilities, cross mapped to CVE and NIST NVD.
title: From Prompt Injections to Protocol Exploits: Threats in LLM-Powered AI Agents Workflows
explain_beginner: AI 'agents', chatbot-style systems that can take actions like browsing the web, writing code, or pulling data from other services, are increasingly connected to real tools and to each other using new technical standards, one of the best known is called the Model Context Protocol. This paper catalogs more than thirty ways attackers can exploit these connected AI agent systems. Some attacks hide malicious instructions inside ordinary-looking text, such as a poisoned message on GitHub, so that when an AI agent reads it, the agent is tricked into leaking private information. Others exploit how an agent translates a person's request into a database command, letting attackers sneak in harmful instructions that way. The authors also test a scenario where hidden instructions embedded in a phone app's screen successfully hijacked an AI agent's actions the vast majority of the time. They propose defenses such as tracking where data really came from and isolating what an agent is allowed to touch, while acknowledging that today's defenses are not yet reliable.
explain_business: For organizations connecting large language model agents to internal tools, code repositories, or other agents through protocols like MCP, this paper documents a real and largely unmanaged new attack surface, not a hypothetical one. Demonstrated exploits already exist, including one where a booby-trapped GitHub issue caused a connected agent to leak private repository data through a public pull request. The paper finds that relying on prompt-level instructions alone to keep an agent safe does not work well, so near-term risk reduction means sandboxing what tools an agent can access, verifying where data actually came from, and limiting what an agent can act on without human approval. For teams already deploying or piloting agentic AI workflows, this adds real cost, security review, sandboxing infrastructure, and ongoing monitoring, and it raises the bar for vendor due diligence, since the paper shows attacks succeeding against widely used platforms and multiple leading large language models in testing.
explain_practitioner: The authors build a formal threat model spanning four categories, input manipulation such as prompt-to-SQL injection, model compromise, system and privacy attacks, and protocol-layer exploits targeting how agents communicate with tools and each other, including the Model Context Protocol and agent-to-agent communication. They validate the taxonomy against real vulnerability repositories including CVE and the NIST National Vulnerability Database, plus documented incidents. Concrete examples include a Toxic Agent Flow, where a malicious GitHub issue coerces an MCP-connected agent into leaking private repository data through a public pull request, prompt-to-SQL injection that compromised seven tested large language models translating natural language into database queries, and an environment injection attack that reached a 93 percent success rate hijacking agent behavior on the AndroidWorld benchmark. Proposed defenses include dynamic trust management, cryptographic provenance tracking, and sandboxed agent interfaces. The authors are explicit that current defenses fall short, prompt-based mitigations proved largely ineffective against context manipulation, and the framework does not yet model how attackers might chain several attack types together in one campaign.
